title: Chapter 3 — When Culture Is Not a System
paragraphs: This is the book's pivotal chapter and the exam's likely centerpiece. It argues that the friction Samoan community workers feel inside US bureaucracies is not a clash of cultures but a clash of reflexivities — a collision between someone who understands himself as connected to a system and someone who understands herself as engaged with a culture. Gershon is emphatic that both parties are cosmopolitan and versatile, so no single "culture" is the backdrop. What differs is how each understands a person's relationship to their role.

The setting: in 1998 NOSA was evicted from its San Francisco office and urgently needed a new home. NOSA housed a community day school for Samoan high-schoolers near dropping out, part of a district network. Alofa, who heads NOSA's branch and runs the classroom, reluctantly approached Ben — the principal over the day schools, himself not Samoan (he came from the Philippines as a child) and the person who controls the school's money and staff. She humbly asked whether one of the district's empty school buildings could become NOSA's new location, a reasonable request since an empty school had already gone to a rival Samoan organization.

Ben said no. He explained at length that he too was "caught in the system" and could not do what he wished, and asked Alofa to accept his refusal because she understood his constraints. That plea for empathy is what insulted her. Leaving furious, she said: "No matai would ever do anything like that." A chief, she explained, would have listened, nodded, and promised to do what he could — accepting responsibility, and never once mentioning how hard his own position was.

The clash, precisely: both share the assumption that people are connected in many ways and that any interaction poses the question of which connections become visible now. The insulting difference is how each relates to a role. For Ben, to fully inhabit his role would be to speak only the system's "no" and sever his human connection to Alofa; he can show connection only by revealing that they are both constrained by, and only partly committed to, a hindering system. For Alofa, Samoans embody a social order — they do not mediate it — and unity comes from how fully one inhabits a role. Refusing to be "the chief of the school" is, to her, antithetical to sociality itself.

Gershon distinguishes two kinds of mediator that governments demand: representatives and translators. Samoans readily supply representatives — this maps onto the matai system, especially the talking chief who makes connections visible — though representation is contentious in diaspora, since no one can legitimately claim to be the chief "of San Francisco." But Samoans reject the translator or cultural-broker role. Drawing on Walter Benjamin, she argues Samoan cultural knowledge lacks the quality of translatability: roles embody values, so listing values like service and respect in a workshop, detached from their situation, is not conveying culture at all.

To explain why systems demand translation, she turns to Luhmann's systems theory — used to model bureaucrats' reflexivity, not reality. Systems recode all outside input into their own terms and treat families as a disordered "environment" to be reorganized. She shows this in a Juvenile Probation training led by Angela, who teaches case managers to treat families "as systems" with equal, transparent information flow. When Gershon and Alofa object that Samoan children are not supposed to voice needs — a child who asks is implicitly criticizing the parent — Angela is simply baffled. From a system-carrier's stance, culture is not a rival social order but a "recodable disorder," an explanation for communication failure that always sits outside the system. The chapter's irony: here, reflexivity builds barriers, not bridges — a matter of second-order reflexivity, our sense of what it means for another person to belong to a social order.
